bios.NX-1001:
Dr. Mara Voss led the NEXUS architecture team from the program's first month, January 1996, and stayed until January 1999 to close the last architectural questions after OER took over. Dr. Voss holds a doctorate in computer engineering, did graduate work in distributed systems, and came to NEXUS as lead architect of a research program that combined observations from independent technical sources.

The interface rules and failure boundaries that the eight regional nodes still follow were set under Dr. Voss's direction. Dr. Voss expected engineers to defend their assumptions, used exact terms and corrected loose ones, and would pause before answering a disputed technical question. The NEXUS engineering room of 1996-98 ran on that standard.

Dr. Voss approved 34 revisions in the Document Register, more than anyone of the NEXUS years: the first machine room plan, FLR-001 A (July 1996); the first power and cooling drawings, PWR-001 A and MEC-001 A (September 1996); the FDDI backbone, NET-001 A (November 1996); the first regional link test, NET-002 A (February 1997); and the commissioning set of June 1998, including the watch floor as built, FLR-002 B.

After the July 1998 commissioning Dr. Voss led the technical handoff to OER's new engineering staff, working most closely with Rebecca Shaw, OER's first in-house architect. Dr. Voss left in January 1999 for Y2K work elsewhere in the program.
bios.NX-1002:
Martin Keene was the NEXUS systems and infrastructure engineer from January 1996 to November 1998. Keene holds a bachelor's degree in computer engineering, trained in Unix and systems administration, and came from research-computing support, where the job was keeping a mix of hardware and the services on it running.

Keene was patient with difficult faults and preferred repair to redesign. Colleagues knew Keene for reading the logs before touching anything and for writing down every command and every configuration difference, so a fix could be repeated by someone else. Keene drew 17 revisions in the Document Register, among them the first machine room plan, FLR-001 A (July 1996), the first power drawing, PWR-001 A, the central host rack, RCK-01 A (July 1997), and the primary and standby host pair, RCK-01 B (March 1998).

Keene set up OER's first host and recovery procedures and worked alongside Mike Dwyer through 1998, handing the servers and storage over before leaving. The OER assignment ended in November 1998, when Keene moved to Y2K remediation work.
bios.NX-1003:
Nate Bell built the network that first tied the eight regional nodes to the center. Bell came to NEXUS in January 1996 with a technical diploma in telecommunications and vendor training in routing, after years as a regional network technician and network implementation engineer.

Bell had a dry sense of humor and was skeptical of vague reports, and above all knew the difference between a dead link, a slow one and an unreliable one. Bell's reports were short and full of readings: interface names, times, loss figures. Bell drew the FDDI backbone, NET-001 A (November 1996), the first T1 links to nodes N1-N8 for acceptance testing, NET-002 A (February 1997), the regional collector room, NODE-001 A, and the as-built drawing of all eight nodes, NODE-001 B (June 1998), nine register revisions in all.

Bell spent the commissioning months of 1998 on regional connectivity and handed the links to Daniel Okafor, who had joined OER that January. The NEXUS assignment ended in October 1998, when Bell moved to urgent Y2K work.
bios.NX-1004:
Yvonne Chen was the NEXUS database and archive specialist from January 1996 to December 1998. Chen holds a bachelor's degree in information science, trained in database administration and archival storage, and came from running the database of a technical research archive, with long experience of backup validation and long-term retention.

Chen wrote OER's first preservation and recovery practices, including the rule that a backup is not valid until a restore has been tested. Chen was protective of source records: original values were kept and doubtful rows were flagged, never quietly corrected. Chen's notes were numbered and named the exact tables and fields, and always separated missing data from invalid data.

In the Document Register Chen checked the software architecture drawings from the first integrated prototype, SWA-001 A (July 1996), through the interface contract of May 1997 and the operational configuration of June 1998, and the first regional transfer contract, SWA-002 A (October 1997). Chen handed the archive to Linda Carver, OER's first database administrator, before leaving in December 1998.
bios.NX-1005:
Elias Trent designed the message and interface layer that moved data between the independent NEXUS platforms. Trent holds a master's degree in computer science and came from distributed-systems research on asynchronous exchanges between independently operated research platforms.

Trent's specialty was what happens between systems: message queues, retries, duplicates and timing differences. Trent's notes were compact and dense with sequence numbers and queue states, and grew longer and more explanatory whenever a fault crossed a system boundary. The regional transfer contract, with its spool, transfer and commit verification, came out of that work.

Trent drew the software architecture set, SWA-001 A to D (1996-98), and the regional transfer contract and state model, SWA-002 A and B (1997-98), and checked the network drawings NET-001 and NET-002 for the same period: twelve register revisions. Tom Alvarez took over the interfaces on joining OER in January 1998. Trent served from January 1996 to November 1998, then moved to Y2K work.
bios.NX-1006:
Caleb Rusk wrote the early health checks and alert logic that OER's monitoring grew from. Rusk holds a bachelor's degree in electrical engineering with instrumentation, scripting and control-system coursework, and came to NEXUS from a research lab, first as an instrumentation technician and then building automated test systems.

Rusk liked turning any repeated check into a script, and liked leaving it running overnight before calling it stable. Rusk's notes used test labels and numbered results, and added follow-up lines when a longer run showed something the first quick check had not. The threshold and scheduled-check habits of the first watch floor began there.

Peter Sloane, OER's first monitoring engineer, took over the scripts in March 1998 and worked alongside Rusk through the commissioning months. Rusk was with NEXUS from January 1996 to October 1998 and then moved to Y2K testing.
bios.NX-1007:
Simone Laurent brought OER's first outside data feeds into the system. Laurent holds a bachelor's degree in telecommunications engineering, trained in data communications and protocol analysis, and came from integrating third-party feeds into a research collection system.

Laurent never blamed an outside provider without evidence, and was careful to separate what a provider said had been sent from what OER actually received; both went in the log, with source names, receipt times, response codes and gaps. When the evidence was incomplete, Laurent's wording said so. That way of writing up a feed problem is still the one the floor uses.

Laurent worked with Marisol Vega, who joined OER in April 1998 to own the external feeds, through the first months of live operations. Laurent served with NEXUS from January 1996 to December 1998.
bios.NX-1008:
Priya Nanduri developed the NEXUS methods for matching reports from independent sources. Nanduri holds a master's degree in applied mathematics with coursework in statistics and information systems, and came from research data engineering on exactly that problem.

Nanduri resisted early conclusions and always asked what comparison would disprove a hypothesis. The working rule was that an overlap in time supports a match, not a common cause; Nanduri's notes were full of phrases such as "consistent with" and "not sufficient to establish", and the correlation desk on the watch floor still works that way. Timestamp normalization and source-quality scoring at OER began with Nanduri's comparisons.

Judy Price, OER's first correlation engineer, joined in March 1998 and learned the methods from Nanduri during the commissioning months. Nanduri served from January 1996 to December 1998, then moved to Y2K work.
bios.NX-1009:
Warren Pike set up controlled release and change approval at NEXUS. Pike holds a bachelor's degree in computer science, trained in software configuration and release management, and came from build and release engineering for a research software group with several test and production environments.

Pike trusted documented repeatability over verbal assurance and worked from numbered checklists with explicit pass or fail lines. A release with an unproven rollback path did not go out, and a request to "just change one thing" got a change number like everything else. That discipline is where OER's change control begins.

Pike checked twelve register revisions: the central host racks RCK-01 A and B (1997-98), the storage and network racks RCK-02 and RCK-03, and the first badge and guard desk drawing, SEC-001 A (May 1996), and drew the first equipment inventories, INV-001 A (July 1997) and INV-002 A. Elaine Foster took over configuration and release in February 1998. Pike served from January 1996 to October 1998.
bios.NX-1010:
Helen Sato defined the access controls and audit trails OER inherited from NEXUS. Sato holds a bachelor's degree in computer science with further training in access control and system auditing, and came from system-integrity work in research environments where every change had to be traceable.

Sato questioned unexplained changes without assuming bad intent, and was known for careful, unsensational findings that separated what the record showed from what it could not show. Each finding named who or what had performed an action, the audit evidence available, and the limits of the investigation.

Sato drew the facility security plan in the Document Register: SEC-001 A (May 1996), with the NX-1 badges, the guard desk and the keyed engineering room, and SEC-001 B (June 1998), when OER-1 laminated badges were issued and worn on the watch floor. Robert Ames took over security in April 1998 and worked alongside Sato that year. Sato served from January 1996 to November 1998.
bios.NX-1011:
Victor Hale measured the operating limits and recovery behavior of the NEXUS system and stayed through January 1999 to finish the handoff to OER engineering. Hale holds a bachelor's degree in electrical engineering with graduate coursework in performance analysis, and came from performance work on research-computing and communications systems.

Hale repeated every measurement before accepting a trend, disliked explanations based on a single observation, and preferred a number to a broad assurance. Reports came with baselines, sample sizes and comparison periods attached, and earlier measurements were revisited whenever test conditions changed.

Hale checked ten register revisions: the machine room and watch floor plans, FLR-001 A and B and FLR-002 A and B (1996-98), the first power and cooling drawings, the regional collector room drawings, NODE-001 A and B, and the first Site B layout, SITE-B-001 A (September 1997). Denise Porter, OER's first reliability engineer, learned the baselines from Hale in 1998. Hale left in January 1999 for Y2K work.
bios.OER-1998-001:
Daniel Okafor was one of the first two engineers OER hired, starting on 7 January 1998, and looked after the links between OER Central and the eight regional nodes until January 2003. Okafor holds a B.S. in electrical engineering with networking coursework and vendor training in routers and wide-area networks, and came from telecommunications network operations: leased circuits, remote facilities and routing equipment.

Okafor was calm under pressure, skeptical of any explanation that could not be tested, and kept topology diagrams with handwritten changes, the circuit number noted beside every outage time. Nate Bell handed the regional links to Okafor in 1998. The watch floor valued Okafor's timing notes; Lucia Ferrante on the Red night crew kept them as a reference.

Okafor drew eight register revisions, most of them the road to the alternate site: DS3 to Site B, NET-002 D (September 1999); the Site B operations room, SITE-B-001 B (October 1999); the Gigabit core that replaced FDDI, NET-001 D (June 2000); OC-3 to Site B and DS3 to every node, NET-002 E (September 2000); and the full watch floor at Site B, SITE-B-001 C and SITE-B-002 C (2002). Okafor left OER on 31 January 2003.
bios.OER-1998-002:
Tom Alvarez joined OER on 7 January 1998, the same day as Daniel Okafor, and maintained the interfaces that let OER's separate sources and services exchange usable data until December 2001. Alvarez holds a B.S. in computer science with integration and Unix scripting training, and came from application development and systems integration, connecting tools that had been built separately.

Elias Trent handed the NEXUS interface layer to Alvarez in 1998. Alvarez was inventive and collaborative and liked a small working fix; every script was kept in dated copies, each with a short comment explaining any unusual workaround. Over four years Alvarez turned many of the fragile conversion routines of the early system into documented ones.

Alvarez drew the rollover configuration of the software architecture, SWA-001 E (November 1999), and the transfer schedule for the new DS3 links, SWA-002 C (September 2000), and checked Okafor's network revisions of 1999-2000. Alvarez left OER on 31 December 2001.
bios.OER-1998-003:
Mike Dwyer looked after OER's servers and storage from February 1998 to January 2003. Dwyer holds a B.S. in computer engineering, trained in Unix administration and hardware maintenance, and came from corporate data-center support, where the job included coordinating hardware repairs with vendors.

Martin Keene handed the NEXUS hosts to Dwyer in 1998. Dwyer built a reputation for repairs that could be repeated and for labeling every cable; a failed part stayed on the shelf until someone knew why it had failed, and the spare-parts notes were always current. Dwyer was patient with machines and with junior staff.

Dwyer drew nine register revisions: the alternate site's generator, UPS and transfer switch, PWR-002 A (August 1999); the larger generator fuel capacity, PWR-001 C (October 1999); the tape vault and spare parts cage, FLR-001 C (November 1999); the Gigabit core switches and the first SAN (2000); the second central host generation, RCK-01 C (January 2001); and the watch floor door reader, FLR-002 C (November 2001). Dwyer left OER on 31 January 2003.
bios.OER-1998-004:
Rebecca Shaw was OER's first in-house systems architect and technical lead, from February 1998 to December 2002. Shaw holds a B.S. in information systems with training in systems operations and project coordination, and came from enterprise IT operations, coordinating deployments, technical handoffs and incident response across several support groups.

Shaw took the architecture over from Dr. Mara Voss in the months after commissioning and coordinated the move from NEXUS development practice to routine operations. Shaw kept an action list beside the terminal and gave every open issue an owner and a due date, and over the years worked steadily at making the system maintainable by the team rather than by a few individual experts.

Shaw approved 21 register revisions, among them the alternate site power plant, PWR-002 A (August 1999), the Site B operations room (October 1999), the rollover configuration, SWA-001 E (November 1999), the Gigabit core (June 2000), the second central host generation (January 2001), the watch floor door reader (November 2001) and the full watch floor at Site B (2002). Shaw left OER on 31 December 2002.
bios.OER-1998-005:
Elaine Foster ran configuration and release from February 1998 to January 2002. Foster holds a B.A. in technical communication with training in configuration control and software release, and came from technical publishing and release coordination for enterprise software, keeping revision histories and deployment instructions.

Warren Pike handed NEXUS change control to Foster in 1998. Foster was organized and diplomatic, disliked undocumented changes but worked constructively with the people who made them, and checked titles, version numbers and file names before closing any task. As the research environment became a service that never stopped, Foster made sure each revision could still be traced back.

Foster drew the inventory for the second central host generation, INV-001 C (January 2001), and checked the guest badge drawing, SEC-001 C (August 2000), the OER-2 magnetic stripe badges, SEC-001 D (November 2001), and the rack revisions of 2000-01. Foster left OER on 31 January 2002.
bios.OER-1998-006:
Linda Carver set up OER's first database and archive handling after NEXUS, from February 1998 to January 1999. Carver holds a B.A. in mathematics with database administration and records-management training, and came from database and records support for a research organization.

Yvonne Chen handed the NEXUS archive to Carver during the commissioning year. Carver was quietly persistent and noticed small discrepancies: paper reconciliation sheets were kept for every batch, incomplete batches were marked, and every unexplained record count was followed up.

Carver was with OER for just under a year, through the first months of live operations. The archive notes Carver left behind were what the team relied on until Martin Feldman arrived in June 2000. Carver left OER on 31 January 1999.
bios.OER-1998-007:
Judy Price built repeatable data-consistency checks across OER's sources and reports from March 1998 to February 2001. Price holds a B.A. in statistics with technical quality assurance training, and came from quality assurance for a data-processing group, reconciling reports and investigating results that did not agree.

Priya Nanduri passed the NEXUS correlation methods on to Price during the commissioning months. Price was patient with complicated discrepancies and never named a pattern until it could be reproduced, keeping before-and-after samples and the exact query used to confirm each one. Price worked hard at telling real anomalies apart from ingestion and timing errors, and the correlation desk's early review rules came from that work.

Price's three years spanned the first full year of operations and Y2K. Price left OER on 28 February 2001.
bios.OER-1998-008:
Peter Sloane wrote and maintained OER's routine checks and automation from March 1998 to February 2003. Sloane holds a B.S. in computer science with Unix operations, scripting and monitoring training, and came from operations-center support, building small monitoring scripts and chasing recurring alerts.

Caleb Rusk handed the NEXUS health checks to Sloane in 1998. Sloane trusted repeated measurements over a single green light, collected alert samples before changing any threshold, and kept a notebook of recurring false alarms. On the watch floor Sloane worked with Raymond Kowalski, the first Red Day Lead, on the early questions about the commit monitor.

Over five years Sloane became especially attentive to intermittent failures that disappeared before anyone could reproduce them, and the floor's habit of logging a short-lived fault even when it has cleared started there. Sloane left OER on 28 February 2003.
bios.OER-1998-009:
Denise Porter established OER's reliability baselines from March 1998 to February 2000. Porter holds a B.S. in electrical engineering with training in performance analysis and fault isolation, and came from computer operations at a university research computing center, investigating recurring slowdowns and intermittent hardware faults.

Victor Hale passed the NEXUS measurements on to Porter. Porter was steady under pressure and disliked early declarations that a problem was fixed; recurring faults went into a small spiral notebook, and current readings were compared with older printouts before anything was closed.

Porter checked six register revisions in 1999, all part of getting through the rollover: the alternate site power plant, PWR-002 A, the generator fuel capacity increase, PWR-001 C, the Site B operations room, SITE-B-001 B, the tape vault, FLR-001 C, the rollover configuration, SWA-001 E, and the first Site B switchover procedure, SITE-B-002 A (December 1999). Porter left OER on 29 February 2000.
bios.OER-1998-010:
Marisol Vega owned OER's external data feeds and carrier relationships from April 1998 to March 2002. Vega holds a B.S. in communications engineering with vendor training in telemetry and modem systems, and came from a regional telecommunications provider, maintaining leased lines, modem banks and third-party data feeds.

Vega started the week before the watch floor opened and learned the NEXUS feeds from Simone Laurent. Vega was patient but skeptical of vendor assurances and preferred evidence to explanations: handwritten carrier contact sheets sat beside the console, and line noise and outage times were noted in the margins.

Vega's four years covered the first outside feeds, the rollover and the busy storm seasons of 1999-2001, when a regional site going quiet often meant a carrier problem first. Vega left OER on 31 March 2002.
bios.OER-1998-011:
Robert Ames was responsible for access control and system integrity from April 1998 to March 2003. Ames holds a B.S. in computer science with corporate security and Unix administration training, and came from Unix administration at a financial services company, where account controls, audit trails and change approvals were part of the job.

Helen Sato handed the NEXUS access controls to Ames in 1998. Ames was reserved and methodical, distrusted undocumented exceptions but avoided needless alarm, numbered every paper binder and annotated each access review with dates and initials.

Ames drew the two security revisions of OER's early years: the guest badge pools, SEC-001 C (August 2000), with cleared badges GC-01 to GC-10 and uncleared GN-01 to GN-10, which started visitor sign-in at the Lead position; and the OER-2 magnetic stripe photo badges with door readers at the watch floor and engineering room, SEC-001 D (November 2001). Ames left OER on 31 March 2003.
bios.OER-1998-012:
Colleen Brannigan held the Blue Crew night COMM seat from the day the watch floor opened, 15 April 1998, until July 2000. Brannigan grew up in Worcester, Massachusetts, studied English at Worcester State, and came to OER from work as an executive assistant and as volunteer coordinator for a nonprofit hotline, where the job was keeping a voice level for people who needed one.

That was the job at OER too. Night COMM takes the outside calls when a regional site goes quiet, and Brannigan's phone log was known for being complete and readable at three in the morning. The spring of 1999 was a busy first test: Node 4 (Gulf / Texas) dropped off on the night of 3 April, Node 8 (Midwest / Great Lakes) went down before dawn on 9 April as tornadoes crossed the Cincinnati area, and Node 5 (Southwest) lost contact on the evening of 3 May as the Oklahoma storms came through. Brannigan was at the COMM desk for all three, and again in September when Hurricane Floyd took Node 3 (Southeast) off the board for nine hours.

Brannigan was a close friend of Joanne Tillman on the Red Day crew, and the two traded notes on phone wording for years. Away from the floor: Irish step dance, mystery novels and long hikes. Brannigan left OER at the end of July 2000.
bios.OER-1998-013:
Deirdre Maddox sat Red Crew day Monitoring in the launch cohort, from 15 April 1998 to the end of March 1999. A Scranton, Pennsylvania native with a B.S. in Information Systems from Penn State and a network-operations certificate, Maddox had worked as a data-center operator for a regional insurer and then as a NOC technician at a telecom carrier before coming to OER.

Monitoring is the seat that watches the board, and Maddox was quick at it: good at seeing a pattern in the receiver data and fast at sorting what mattered from what did not. Maddox worked the first summer of live operations, when the floor was still learning which displays to trust, and helped write down what a normal day looked like so the next crew could compare.

Maddox learned the floor under Raymond Kowalski, the Red Day Lead, and took Kowalski's habits about clean handoffs to heart. New staff remember Maddox as the person who explained the systems patiently, twice if needed. Off shift: half-marathons, cross-stitch and Pennsylvania Dutch cooking. Maddox left OER on 31 March 1999.
bios.OER-1998-014:
Farah Siddiqui worked Blue Crew night Monitoring from the opening of the watch floor in April 1998 to May 1999. Siddiqui grew up in Dearborn, Michigan, earned a B.S. in Electrical Engineering from the University of Michigan-Dearborn, and came to OER from a test-engineering job at an automotive supplier and a stint leading a help desk.

On the floor Siddiqui brought real technical depth to the Monitoring seat and a habit of asking why a reading looked the way it did until the answer made sense. The spring of 1999 kept the Blue night crew busy: Siddiqui was on the board when Node 4 (Gulf / Texas) went dark on the night of 3 April, when Node 8 (Midwest / Great Lakes) dropped before dawn on 9 April, and when Node 5 (Southwest) lost contact during the storms of 3 May.

Siddiqui was a friend of Lucia Ferrante on the Red night crew; the two compared notes across shifts. Outside work: coaching youth soccer, calligraphy and family cooking. Siddiqui left OER at the end of May 1999.
bios.OER-1998-015:
Gideon Marsh was the Red Crew floater in the launch cohort, from 15 April 1998 to February 1999. Marsh came from Boise, Idaho, with a B.S. in Industrial Technology and a Red Cross first-aid instructor certification, after years as a plant operations technician and several fire seasons as a wildland-fire dispatcher.

The floater covers whatever seat is empty, and Marsh was the rare person who was comfortable in every one of them: Lead, Monitoring, Correlation or COMM, day or night. In the first months of the floor, when the procedures were new and the crews were still settling, Marsh's easy manner and good stories helped keep the room steady.

Marsh was close with Raymond Kowalski, the Red Day Lead, and got on well with everyone on the crew. Away from the floor Marsh fly-fished, carved wood and rode a motorcycle through the national parks. Marsh left OER at the end of February 1999.
bios.OER-1998-016:
Harold Pruitt was the first Blue Crew Day Lead, from the opening of the watch floor on 15 April 1998 until the end of January 2004. A native of Birmingham, Alabama, Pruitt held a B.S. in Industrial Management and Army Signal Corps training, served as an Army signals officer with the rank of captain, and then spent fifteen years running operations at a long-distance telephone switching center.

Pruitt ran the Blue day shift the way a switching center is run: calmly, courteously and by the procedure, with directives worded so precisely they rarely needed a second reading. Pruitt had the floor through the California rolling blackouts of 2001, when Node 6 (California) lost power on 17 January, 19 March and 8 May, and through Hurricane Lili's pass over Node 4 (Gulf / Texas) on 3 October 2002. Pruitt trained Rodney Goodwin, Denny Abernathy, Craig Lowry and Yvette Colbert, and mentored Imani Rhodes.

Pruitt's last log entry, on 28 January 2004, noted that the binder was current and that Lowry had the keys to the supply cabinet. Outside work Pruitt sang bass in a gospel quartet, played correspondence chess and volunteered at church. Franklin Peralta and Derek Sheridan were close friends on the floor. Pruitt left OER on 31 January 2004.
bios.OER-1998-017:
Hector Salazar was a founding member of the Red Crew day watch: Correlation from 15 April 1998, then Red Day Lead from May 2001 until July 2002. Salazar grew up in El Paso, Texas, earned an A.S. in Electronics Technology, learned statistics on the side, and spent seventeen years in a defense contractor's records-reconciliation group before a short stint in freight logistics.

Correlation is the seat that decides whether two reports describe the same thing, and Salazar was known for refusing to force a match: the answer was always to ask for the second source. Salazar was on watch when Node 8 (Midwest / Great Lakes) lost power in the Chicago heat of 30 July 1999, when the Nisqually earthquake took Node 7 (Pacific Northwest) off the board on 28 February 2001, and as Lead on 11 September 2001, when the day crew ran the personnel accountability contacts and kept every console staffed. In June 2002 Salazar had the floor when the Rodeo-Chediski fire cut Node 5 (Southwest).

Salazar trained Colette Wexler, Amanda Mitchell and Lorraine Varga, and kept a standing lunch with Raymond Kowalski and Walter Dunmore. At home: small-cabinet woodworking, boxing history and Tex-Mex cooking. Salazar left OER on 31 July 2002.
bios.OER-1998-018:
Imani Rhodes sat Blue Crew day Monitoring from the first day of the watch floor, 15 April 1998, to the end of June 2006: eight years at the same desk. Rhodes grew up in Oakland, California, earned a B.S. in Computer Information Systems at San Jose State, and worked as a NOC technician at an internet service provider and in wire-transfer operations at a bank.

Rhodes read dashboards faster than almost anyone on the floor and was a natural trainer: Derek Sheridan, Phyllis Acosta and Keith Espinoza all learned the job from Rhodes, and Paula Ocampo leaned on Rhodes in the first year. Harold Pruitt was Rhodes's own mentor. On the Blue day crew Rhodes was on the board for the Fort Worth tornado evening of 28 March 2000, the California rolling blackouts of 2001 and Hurricane Lili on 3 October 2002.

Rhodes laughed easily and protected the crew's morale on long days. The last log line from the desk, on 30 June 2006, noted leaving it on a quiet Friday, "which is the best kind". Off the floor: jazz piano, cycling and community theater. Jerome Atwater was a friend and a frequent shift-swap partner.
bios.OER-1998-019:
Jerome Atwater held the Blue Crew night Correlation seat from the opening of the floor in April 1998 until February 2004. Atwater grew up in Baton Rouge, Louisiana, earned a B.S. in Computer Science at Southern University and a database-administration certificate, and worked as a database operator at a state agency while serving as a volunteer firefighter.

Atwater was a careful correlation analyst who could explain a complicated night in two sentences and kept a sense of humor when the board was busy. Atwater was on the night desk for a long list of first-year events: Node 4 (Gulf / Texas) on 3 April 1999, the Cincinnati tornado night that took Node 8 down on 9 April, the Oklahoma storms of 3 May, Hurricane Floyd on Node 3 (Southeast) that September, and the Hector Mine earthquake that briefly cut Node 6 (California) on 16 October 1999. In December 2002 the Carolinas ice storm kept Node 3 down for almost fourteen hours of Atwater's shift.

Leonard Fitch mentored Atwater and stayed a friend, and Atwater swapped shifts often with Imani Rhodes. Atwater's last line from the desk, on 28 February 2004, read: "Correlation remains a matter of evidence, not of feeling." Off shift: gumbo, bass guitar and fishing.
bios.OER-1998-020:
Joanne Tillman was one of the first crew of April 1998 and spent more than ten years on the Red day watch: COMM from 15 April 1998, then Red Day Lead from September 2002 until the end of November 2008. Tillman grew up in Duluth, Minnesota, studied Communication at the University of Minnesota Duluth, and came to OER after eighteen months as a county 911 dispatcher and a job at a radio station.

Tillman was precise and friendly on the phone and could not stand a silent line. As COMM, Tillman took the calls through the Chicago heat outage of July 1999, the Nisqually earthquake in February 2001 and 11 September 2001; as Lead, Tillman ran the floor through the November 2002 tornado outbreak in the Midwest and the May 2003 storms that took Node 8 (Midwest / Great Lakes) off the board. Tillman trained the COMM seat for a generation of the Red day crew: Marisa Harlan, Sandra Lacey, Charlene Tierney and Tamara Ortiz.

Tillman kept standing lunches with Walter Dunmore and Jeffrey Underhill and was a close friend of Colleen Brannigan. On 30 November 2008 the day watch said goodbye to one of the first crew with cake at 15:00. Off the floor: choir, downhill skiing and knitting.
bios.OER-1998-021:
Leonard Fitch was the Blue Crew Night Lead for sixteen years, from the opening of the floor on 15 April 1998 to the end of May 2014. A Rochester, New York native, Fitch held an A.A.S. in Electrical Technology and Navy electronics training, served as a Navy electronics technician, and spent twelve years reading substation telemetry at a regional power-grid control center.

That background gave Fitch an instinct for power and timing that the night crew relied on. Fitch was the Lead for the storm nights of spring 1999, Hurricane Floyd on Node 3 (Southeast), the Hector Mine earthquake on 16 October 1999, the December 2002 Carolinas ice storm and the Presidents' Day blizzard that took Node 2 (Mid-Atlantic) down on 17 February 2003. Fitch trained Franklin Peralta, Lamar Iverson, Brenda Ellison and Gail Everett, and mentored Jerome Atwater.

Fitch was terse, unflappable and quietly generous, with a dark sense of humor that steadied a long night. Marcellus Granger was a friend and a frequent shift-swap partner. Away from work: ham radio, vegetable canning and hockey. Fitch left OER on 31 May 2014, and Lamar Iverson took the seat.
bios.OER-1998-022:
Lucia Ferrante watched the Red Crew night board from 15 April 1998 until 31 December 2002. Ferrante grew up in Providence, Rhode Island, earned a B.S. in Physics at the University of Rhode Island, served four years as an Air Force weather officer and then in the Reserve, and worked as a process-monitoring technician at a semiconductor fab and as a hospital telemetry technician.

Ferrante noticed small drifts before anyone else did and wrote strong, exact notes; engineer Daniel Okafor's timing notes were a favorite reference. Ferrante was on the Monitoring desk for the Y2K rollover night, taking the scheduled commit-monitor readings as the date boundary passed, and for the Christmas 2000 ice storm that kept Node 4 (Gulf / Texas) down for more than nine hours on 26 December.

In November 2002 Ferrante received orders back to active military service as a weather officer; the last watch, on 31 December 2002, closed out a seat Ferrante had held since opening day. Off shift: backyard astronomy, bread baking and family Italian-American recipes. Farah Siddiqui was a friend from the first year.
bios.OER-1998-023:
Paula Ocampo took the Blue Crew day COMM seat in the launch cohort and held it from 15 April 1998 to the end of that year. Ocampo grew up in San Antonio, Texas, studied Communication at the University of Texas at San Antonio, and came to OER from supervising bilingual customer service at a utility, with part-time work assisting a court interpreter.

Ocampo was warm, steady and careful with wording, and brought a diplomat's touch to the outside calls of the first year of operations. Being bilingual made Ocampo the person the crew turned to when a regional contact was easier to reach in Spanish.

Imani Rhodes, on the Monitoring desk next door, mentored Ocampo through the first months of live operations. Outside work Ocampo danced salsa, gardened and hosted large family gatherings. Ocampo left OER on 31 December 1998.
bios.OER-1998-024:
Raymond Kowalski was the first Red Crew Day Lead, from the opening of the watch floor on 15 April 1998 until the end of March 2000. Kowalski grew up in Toledo, Ohio, retired from the Air Force in 1993 as a master sergeant after twenty years in communications-center operations, and then spent five years as a shift supervisor at a regional utility control room.

Kowalski spoke last in a room, rarely raised a voice and believed in the procedure; the clean handoff the Red crew still uses started with Kowalski. Kowalski worked with engineer Peter Sloane on the early questions about the commit monitor and had the floor on 30 July 1999, when the Chicago heat took Node 8 (Midwest / Great Lakes) off utility power. Kowalski mentored Deirdre Maddox and trained Curtis Mendez, whose last log line years later recalled Kowalski's warning that the tiles lie sometimes, and that Kowalski had been right about which ones.

Kowalski kept a standing lunch with Hector Salazar and was close with Gideon Marsh. Off duty: fishing on Lake Erie, restoring old transistor radios and crossword puzzles. Kowalski left OER on 31 March 2000.
bios.OER-1998-025:
Renata Voigt has been on the Red Crew night watch since the floor opened on 15 April 1998: twenty-eight years in the night COMM seat, and Red Night Lead since October 2026. Voigt grew up in Fargo, North Dakota, earned an associate degree in office technology, took evening linguistics courses, and came to OER from a cellular provider's call center and a receptionist's desk.

Voigt's clear diction and patience with upset callers made the night COMM seat what it is. Voigt took the calls on the 1999/2000 rollover night, through the Christmas 2000 ice storm on Node 4 (Gulf / Texas), Tropical Storm Allison in June 2001, Hurricane Ivan on Node 3 (Southeast) in 2004, Sandy in October 2012 and the GPS week rollover in April 2019. Voigt trained Whitney Haddad, Cecil Eaton and Morgan Hammond, and Walter Dunmore looked out for Voigt in the early years.

Voigt carpools with Trevor Jessup and is a friend of Leo Halloran. Off shift: language learning, birdwatching and roller derby. No one on the floor has been there longer.
bios.OER-1998-026:
Stuart Lindgren held the Blue Crew day Correlation seat in the launch cohort, from 15 April 1998 to the end of January 1999. Lindgren grew up in Madison, Wisconsin, earned an M.S. in Statistics at the University of Wisconsin-Madison, and worked as a research assistant in a state environmental-monitoring program and as a quality analyst at a paper mill.

Lindgren brought rigorous correlation reasoning to the first months of the floor and documented everything; the index cards in Lindgren's shirt pocket became a small legend. Much of the early wording about what counts as the same event, and what does not, came out of discussions between Lindgren and Hector Salazar on the Red crew.

Lindgren was reserved and quietly funny. Off the floor: birding, trout fishing and the fiddle. Lindgren left OER on 31 January 1999.
bios.OER-1998-027:
Terrence Garrity held the Red Crew night Correlation seat for fourteen years, from the opening of the floor on 15 April 1998 until the end of July 2012. Garrity grew up in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, earned a B.S. in Mathematics at Duquesne University, and spent eight years as an insurance claims-data analyst and two in production control at a steel mill.

Garrity argued like a lawyer, linked records across sources with precise reasoning and stayed calm when challenged. Garrity was on the correlation desk on the 1999/2000 rollover night, during the Christmas 2000 ice storm on Node 4 (Gulf / Texas), Tropical Storm Allison in June 2001 and Hurricane Ivan on Node 3 (Southeast) in September 2004. On 30 June 2012 Garrity watched correlation run slow for about forty minutes after the leap second until Engineering restarted the servers.

Walter Dunmore groomed Garrity for the night crew, and Garrity trained Valerie Tate, who later led it. The last line from the desk, on 31 July 2012, noted that correlation was quiet, just as on the first day. Off shift: club chess, steelworker labor history and baseball statistics.
bios.OER-1998-028:
Tobias Lund started as the Blue Crew floater in the launch cohort of April 1998 and moved to Blue day Correlation in April 1999, staying until January 2001. Lund grew up in Anchorage, Alaska, earned a B.S. in Computer Science at the University of Alaska Fairbanks, and worked as an oil-field systems technician and a remote-site communications installer.

Lund was resourceful in odd conditions, which suited the floater's job of covering whatever seat was empty, and later brought the same calm to correlation. Lund was at the correlation desk on 28 March 2000, when the Fort Worth tornado knocked Node 4 (Gulf / Texas) off the board for the evening, and on 17 January 2001, the first of the California rolling blackouts that cut Node 6.

Lund was quiet and dry and preferred to solve a problem before talking about it. Away from work: backcountry skiing, shortwave listening and baking. Lund left OER on 31 January 2001.
bios.OER-1998-029:
Walter Dunmore led the Red Crew night watch for twelve years, from the opening of the floor on 15 April 1998 until the end of May 2010. Dunmore grew up in Macon, Georgia, served as a Navy radioman in the Vietnam era, and then spent twenty-four years as a telephone central-office technician.

Dunmore was gruff, formal and protective of the crew, called everyone by surname and kept thorough logs. Dunmore had the floor on the 1999/2000 rollover night, through the Christmas 2000 ice storm on Node 4 (Gulf / Texas), Tropical Storm Allison in June 2001 and Hurricane Ivan's night on Node 3 (Southeast) in September 2004. A patient teacher of young operators, Dunmore trained Angela Vail, Jared Lennox and Reuben Schaefer, groomed Terrence Garrity and looked out for Renata Voigt.

Dunmore kept standing lunches with Joanne Tillman and Hector Salazar. The last entry from the seat, on 30 May 2010, said the checklist was in the top drawer with a note for the successor. Off duty: gospel radio, vegetable gardening and model trains. Dunmore retired on 31 May 2010.
bios.OER-1999-001:
Dale Yates held the Blue Crew day COMM seat from March to December 1999. Yates grew up in Lexington, Kentucky, had military technical training and an A.A.S. in electronics, and served four years as an Air Force communications specialist before coming to OER.

Yates arrived after Paula Ocampo's departure and kept the Blue day calls moving through a busy first full year of operations, including the long run-up to Y2K. Yates was cheerful, reliable on overnight cover and good at chasing down an odd fault on a phone line or a regional circuit. That year also brought the first revisions of the operator procedures, including the rule that a transport acknowledgement is not the same thing as archive confirmation.

Outside work Yates played chess and fixed old cars. Yates left OER on 31 December 1999, the last day before the rollover.
bios.OER-1999-002:
Rodney Goodwin was the Blue Crew floater from April to November 1999. Goodwin came from Sacramento, California, with a B.S. in Industrial Technology from California State University, Sacramento, and had trained in a power-plant control room.

Harold Pruitt trained Goodwin on the floor, and it showed: Goodwin wrote clear handoff notes, stayed steady under pressure and asked for the second source before closing anything. As floater Goodwin covered every Blue seat in turn during the busy months of 1999. That autumn the floor was getting ready for Y2K, with a change freeze, a rollover binder and named staffing for 31 December, and Goodwin's careful notes were part of how the Blue crew kept track of it all.

Away from the floor Goodwin sang in a choir and was a licensed amateur radio operator. Goodwin left OER on 30 November 1999.
bios.OER-1999-003:
Curtis Mendez sat Red Crew day Monitoring for six years, from May 1999 to the end of June 2005. Mendez grew up in Hartford, Connecticut, earned a B.S. in Information Technology at the University of Hartford, and worked as an operations clerk in a bank wire room.

Raymond Kowalski trained Mendez on the desk, and Mendez remembered past incidents better than anyone and wrote precise log entries. Mendez was on the Monitoring desk when the Chicago heat took Node 8 (Midwest / Great Lakes) off utility power on 30 July 1999, when the Nisqually earthquake cut Node 7 (Pacific Northwest) on 28 February 2001, on 11 September 2001, during the Rodeo-Chediski fire on Node 5 (Southwest) in June 2002 and through the tornado outbreaks of November 2002 and May 2003.

Mendez's last log line, on 28 June 2005, recalled that Kowalski had said the tiles lie sometimes, and had been right about which ones. Off shift: chess and painting.
bios.OER-1999-004:
Monica Dupree was the Red Crew floater from July 1999 to the end of September 2001. Dupree grew up in Tucson, Arizona, earned a B.S. in Mathematics at the University of Arizona, and worked as a radio dispatcher for a trucking company.

Dupree loved a clean log and was quick to learn new tools, which made the floater's job of moving between seats a good fit. Dupree covered the Red seats through the Y2K period, the change window on the archive host in September 2000 and the summer of 2001, when the floor first logged regional displays that stopped updating.

Dupree had a sharp eye for small timing drifts on the board. Away from work: volunteering at a food bank and gardening. Dupree left OER on 30 September 2001.
bios.OER-1999-005:
Denny Abernathy was the Blue Crew floater from December 1999 to the end of June 2000. Abernathy grew up in Anchorage, Alaska, had military technical training and an A.A.S. in electronics, and served four years as an Army signal specialist.

Harold Pruitt trained Abernathy, who joined the Blue crew just in time for the rollover month. Abernathy was reserved and deeply loyal, good at cross-checking records and quick to pick up the tools on each seat. Abernathy's first weeks were the most closely watched of the floor's first two years: the rollover binder arrived on 16 December 1999, the change freeze ran through the new year, and every Blue seat had to be covered by name. Abernathy covered them through the winter and the spring of 2000.

Off the floor Abernathy played guitar and fixed old cars. Abernathy left OER on 30 June 2000.
bios.OER-2000-001:
Craig Lowry joined the Blue Crew day watch on 1 January 2000, the first day after the rollover, and has been there since: COMM until July 2007 and Blue Day Lead from August 2007. Lowry grew up in Tulsa, Oklahoma, earned an A.S. in Telecommunications Technology, and came to OER from supervising shifts at a regional call center.

Harold Pruitt trained Lowry and, on leaving in 2004, left Lowry the keys to the supply cabinet. As COMM, Lowry took the calls through the Fort Worth tornado of March 2000, the California rolling blackouts of 2001 and Hurricane Lili in October 2002. As Lead, Lowry has run the Blue day shift for nearly two decades and trained Shane Baptiste, Marvin Poole, Irene Donahue and Marcellus Granger.

Lowry is warm and chatty, calm on the phone and good at spotting a small timing drift. Lowry keeps standing lunches with Russell Saldana and Taylor Thatcher. Away from the floor: camping and cooking for large groups.
bios.OER-2000-002:
Franklin Peralta sat Blue Crew night Monitoring from February 2000 to the end of March 2003. Peralta grew up in Jackson, Mississippi, studied Communication at Jackson State University and worked three years as a county 911 dispatcher.

Leonard Fitch trained Peralta on the night desk. Peralta was laid-back and hard to rattle, with a dry humor that kept the night crew going, and had a good eye for timing drifts on the board. Peralta was on Monitoring through the December 2002 Carolinas ice storm, which kept Node 3 (Southeast) down for fourteen hours, and the Presidents' Day blizzard that took Node 2 (Mid-Atlantic) off the board on 17 February 2003.

Peralta was a close friend of Harold Pruitt. Off shift: painting and softball. Peralta left OER on 31 March 2003.
bios.OER-2000-003:
Thomas "Tom" Mercer joined OER in March 2000 as reliability and performance engineer, a month after Denise Porter left, and stayed until August 2006. Mercer holds a B.S. in computer engineering with continuing education in operating-system performance and capacity planning, and came from supporting enterprise Unix systems and transaction-processing services.

Mercer was patient but unsentimental about systems: aging equipment was fine as long as its behavior was understood. Mercer recorded before-and-after measurements, repeated tests under comparable load, noted what did not change as carefully as what did, and often wrote "same load, same result" in the log.

Mercer signed 26 register revisions, the most of any engineer of that decade. Mercer drew Row D for the correlation cluster, FLR-001 D (September 2003), the console network, NET-005 A (January 2004), the flat panel monitors and first video wall, FLR-002 D (March 2004), and the 300 kVA UPS units, PWR-001 D (August 2004), and checked the hot and cold aisles of 2004, the second generator of 2005 and Row E for the blade chassis, FLR-001 F (August 2006). Elaine Brooks succeeded Mercer.
bios.OER-2000-004:
Martin Feldman became OER's dedicated database and archive administrator in June 2000, after the role had been vacant since Linda Carver left, and held it until November 2006. Feldman holds a BS in information systems with database administration training, and came from a research computing group with long retention requirements, managing relational databases, backups and recovery tests.

Feldman was reliable and conservative and preferred a tested recovery path to an unverified optimization. Backup logs and restore notes were kept for every run, completion reports were checked against the actual output, and archived media were tested now and then to make sure they could still be read. As the stored event data grew year by year, Feldman's recovery documentation grew with it.

Feldman checked the transfer schedule for the DS3 links, SWA-002 C (September 2000), and the move of correlation onto the new cluster, SWA-001 F (May 2004). Feldman left OER in November 2006 for a database operations role with a larger research organization.
bios.OER-2000-005:
Colette Wexler served as Red Crew Day Lead from July to December 2000, between Raymond Kowalski's departure and Hector Salazar's move to the Lead seat. Wexler grew up in Charlotte, North Carolina, earned a B.S. in Industrial Technology at UNC Charlotte, and worked as a quality analyst at a utility.

Hector Salazar trained Wexler, who brought an easygoing manner and a dry wit to the Red day floor. Wexler led the crew through the archive host change window of September 2000 and the new nightly archive check times that followed. Wexler's six months as Lead also covered the start of visitor sign-in at the Lead position in September 2000, with every guest badge number written into the watch log.

Wexler was reliable, calm on the phone and steady through long shifts. Away from work: choir and softball. Wexler left OER on 31 December 2000.
bios.OER-2000-006:
Lamar Iverson spent eighteen years on the Blue Crew night watch: COMM from September 2000 to June 2014, then Blue Night Lead until the end of September 2018. Iverson grew up in Denver, Colorado, earned a B.S. in Business Administration at Colorado State University, and supervised shifts at a regional call center before OER.

Leonard Fitch trained Iverson, and Iverson succeeded Fitch as Lead. Iverson took the night calls through the Carolinas ice storm of December 2002, Hurricane Isabel on Node 2 (Mid-Atlantic) in September 2003, Hurricane Frances in 2004, Katrina and Rita on Node 4 (Gulf / Texas) in 2005 and Hurricane Ike in September 2008. Iverson trained Glenn Rowan, Quincy Paxton, Jessica Merritt and Tobiah Gallo.

Iverson loved a clean log, chose words carefully and was calm on the phone. Off shift: amateur radio and camping. Iverson left OER on 30 September 2018.
bios.OER-2000-007:
Yvette Colbert was the Blue Crew floater from November 2000 to the end of June 2001. Colbert grew up in Akron, Ohio, earned an A.S. in Telecommunications Technology, and worked as a radio dispatcher for a trucking company.

Harold Pruitt trained Colbert, who was formal, courteous and steady under pressure, and picked up the tools of each seat quickly. Colbert covered the Blue seats through the winter and spring of 2001, including the California rolling blackouts. Colbert arrived just after the archive host's nightly write times were reset, and learned the new 30-minute alert line along with the rest of the floor. The 2001 California rolling blackouts, which took Node 6 off utility power three times that winter and spring, were Colbert's first real test on the floor.

Away from work Colbert volunteered at a food bank and rode a bicycle. Colbert left OER on 30 June 2001.
bios.OER-2001-001:
Amanda Mitchell sat Red Crew day Correlation from May 2001 to the end of September 2002. Mitchell grew up in Columbus, Ohio, studied English at Ohio State University, and supervised data entry at an insurance carrier before OER.

Hector Salazar trained Mitchell on the correlation desk. Mitchell was laid-back and hard to rattle, with a dry humor and a gift for teaching new staff. Mitchell was on the correlation desk on 11 September 2001 and during the Rodeo-Chediski fire that cut Node 5 (Southwest) on 18 June 2002.

In August 2002 Mitchell gave notice to begin military service; on the final shift, 28 September 2002, the crew shared a cake in the break room at turnover. Off shift: gardening and amateur radio.
bios.OER-2001-002:
Derek Sheridan held the Blue Crew day Correlation seat from May 2001 to the end of May 2005. Sheridan grew up in Laredo, Texas, earned a B.S. in Industrial Technology at Texas A&M International University, and worked as a help-desk technician at a manufacturer.

Imani Rhodes trained Sheridan, who was brisk, direct and wrote precise log entries. Sheridan was on correlation for the third California rolling blackout on 8 May 2001, Hurricane Lili on Node 4 (Gulf / Texas) in October 2002, the storms on Node 5 (Southwest) in May 2003 and Hurricane Charley on Node 3 (Southeast) on 13 August 2004.

Sheridan was a friend and frequent shift-swap partner of Harold Pruitt and kept a standing lunch with Gail Everett. Off shift: baking and birdwatching. Sheridan left OER on 31 May 2005.
bios.OER-2001-003:
Lorraine Varga spent more than twenty-one years on the Red Crew day watch: floater from October 2001, Monitoring from August 2005 and Red Day Lead from January 2009 until April 2023. Varga grew up in Duluth, Minnesota, earned an A.S. in Computer Networking, and worked as a network technician at a cable company.

Hector Salazar trained Varga, and Varga became one of the floor's most important trainers in turn: Pamela Crawley, Nicole Mathis, Dominic Landry and Trevor Jessup all learned the job from Varga. Varga checked the clocks at the leap second of 31 December 2005 and, as Lead, ran the first morning of pandemic precautions on 16 March 2020, with every other console in use and handover by phone bridge.

Varga was earnest, careful and reliable, with precise log entries. Jeffrey Underhill was a friend, and Varga carpooled with Leo Halloran. Off shift: baking and board games. Varga left OER on 30 April 2023.
bios.OER-2001-004:
Brenda Ellison was the Blue Crew floater from December 2001 to the end of July 2002. Ellison grew up in Rochester, New York, earned a B.S. in Information Technology at the Rochester Institute of Technology, and trained in a power-plant control room.

Leonard Fitch trained Ellison, who was reserved, loyal and reliable at overnight hours, with precise log entries. Ellison joined just after the badge re-issue of late 2001 and covered the Blue seats through the following winter and spring. Those were the first months of the new photo badges and door readers, and of the revised handover wording that still asks a watchstander to say whether a status was checked or carried forward. Ellison learned the floor in that period and wrote it down the new way from the start.

Away from the floor Ellison cooked for large groups and baked. Ellison left OER on 31 July 2002.
bios.OER-2002-001:
Nora Whitcomb spent more than eleven years in OER engineering, from January 2002 to August 2013: first as data quality and correlation engineer, then from January 2006 as data integration and interface engineer. Whitcomb holds a BS in computer science with graduate coursework in distributed computing and statistical analysis, and came from a telecommunications network research group, reconciling event reports from switches and network-management systems.

Whitcomb was skeptical without being obstructive and persistent when sources disagreed, and preferred a defensible answer to a quick one. Source timestamps were compared before any match was accepted, unusual cases were annotated, and a running list of unresolved edge cases was kept for years.

That knowledge of where sources disagree made the move to integration natural when Gregory Bennett left at the end of 2005; Whitcomb then applied it to interfaces and data transformation, and Claire Donnelly took over the correlation work. Whitcomb left OER on 31 August 2013, and Eric Matsuda took over the interfaces in 2014.
bios.OER-2002-002:
Graham Whitaker ran configuration and release from February 2002 to June 2006, following Elaine Foster. Whitaker holds a B.S. in computer information systems with training in software configuration management and Unix administration, and came from build and configuration work for an enterprise software team.

Whitaker was firm about process but understood that an emergency repair sometimes comes before the paperwork. Release notes were numbered, deployed files were compared against the approved baselines, and a copy of the last known-good configuration was saved before every change.

Whitaker signed 15 register revisions during the correlation cluster project: drawing the cluster racks, RCK-04 A to D (2003-04), including the April 2004 withdrawal of revision B when correlation went back to the central host, and its return to the cluster that May; drawing the 40 TB SAN, RCK-02 D (October 2003); and approving the cluster network, NET-001 E, the console network, NET-005 A, and OC-12 to Site B, NET-002 F (2003-04). Whitaker left OER on 30 June 2006.
bios.OER-2002-003:
Gail Everett joined the Blue Crew as floater in September 2002 and held the Blue night Correlation seat from May 2004 to the end of April 2011. Everett grew up in Albany, New York, earned a B.S. in Geography (GIS) at SUNY Albany, and worked as a data-center operator.

Leonard Fitch trained Everett. On the night correlation desk Everett worked through Hurricane Frances on Node 3 (Southeast) in September 2004, Katrina and Rita on Node 4 (Gulf / Texas) in 2005, Hurricane Ike in September 2008 and the Pacific tsunami bulletin of 11 March 2011. Everett's GIS background made it natural to think about where a report came from, not only what it said.

Everett was cheerful, good at odd faults and quick with a joke on a long night. Marvin Poole was a friend, and Everett kept a standing lunch with Derek Sheridan. Off shift: choir and running. Everett left OER on 30 April 2011.
bios.OER-2002-004:
Marisa Harlan held the Red Crew day COMM seat from September 2002 to the end of March 2005. Harlan grew up in Buffalo, New York, earned a B.S. in Computer Science at SUNY Buffalo State, and worked as a call-center trainer.

Joanne Tillman trained Harlan on the COMM seat Tillman had just left for the Lead. Harlan wrote clear handoff notes and was a patient teacher. Harlan took the calls through the Veterans Day tornado outbreak of November 2002 and the May 2003 storms on Node 8 (Midwest / Great Lakes), and on 14 August 2003 worked the phones through the Northeast and Great Lakes blackout, while two regional sites ran on generator.

Harlan was gentle and a good listener. Off shift: running and birdwatching. Harlan left OER on 31 March 2005.
bios.OER-2002-005:
Gregory Bennett took on OER's data interfaces in September 2002, after eight months with the seat empty, and held them until December 2005. Bennett holds a BS in computer science with training in enterprise application integration and databases, and came from application integration at a regional financial services company, resolving mismatched formats, identifiers and timing between systems.

Bennett was patient with complicated interfaces and disliked recurring errors being dismissed as normal. Sample payloads and failed transactions were kept, every field mapping was documented, and recovery after an interrupted job was tested as carefully as a normal transfer. Bennett worked across regional feeds whose formats had changed independently for years.

With no architect on staff in 2003-04, Bennett approved twelve register revisions for the correlation cluster: Row D, FLR-001 D, the cluster racks RCK-04 A to C, the SAN, the second collector rack at each node, NODE-001 C, and the flat panel watch floor, FLR-002 D (March 2004), and drew the move of correlation onto the cluster, SWA-001 F (May 2004). Bennett left in December 2005 for a senior enterprise integration role.
bios.OER-2003-001:
Angela Vail sat Red Crew night Monitoring for thirteen years, from February 2003 to the end of February 2016. Vail grew up in Springfield, Illinois, earned a B.S. in Electrical Engineering Technology at the University of Illinois Springfield, and worked as a hospital systems administrator.

Walter Dunmore trained Vail on the night desk. Vail was formal, courteous and careful with records, and reliable overnight. Vail was on the board for Hurricane Ivan's night on Node 3 (Southeast) in September 2004, the leap second of 30 June 2012 and Sandy on 29 October 2012, when Nodes 1 and 2 ran on generator.

The last line from the seat, on 28 February 2016, closed thirteen years of Red nights and left the desk lamp for the next person. Dominic Landry was a friend. Off shift: fixing old cars and board games.
bios.OER-2003-002:
Jeffrey Underhill held the Red Crew day Correlation seat from June 2003 to the end of September 2007. Underhill grew up in Cleveland, Ohio, earned an A.S. in Information Technology, and worked as a hospital systems administrator.

Underhill was calm and dry and good at taking the heat out of a tense call. Two months into the job, on 14 August 2003, Underhill was on correlation as the Northeast and Great Lakes blackout spread, sorting out which regional reports were real outages and which were sites switching to generator. Underhill also worked the leap second of 31 December 2005.

Underhill was a friend of Lorraine Varga and kept a standing lunch with Joanne Tillman. Off shift: running and chess. Underhill left OER on 30 September 2007.
bios.OER-2003-003:
Rhonda Kimball sat Blue Crew night Monitoring from July 2003 to the end of June 2009. Kimball grew up in Norfolk, Virginia, earned an A.S. in Electronics Technology, and worked as an operator at an alarm-monitoring station.

Kimball was blunt but fair, wrote clear handoff notes and read ambiguous data carefully. Kimball was on the board for Hurricane Isabel on Node 2 (Mid-Atlantic) in September 2003, Hurricane Frances on Node 3 (Southeast) in 2004, Hurricane Rita on Node 4 (Gulf / Texas) in September 2005 and Hurricane Ike in September 2008, when Node 4 was down for most of two days. Kimball's handoffs were known for saying exactly what had and had not been confirmed at the end of a long night.

Off shift Kimball read local history and watched birds. Kimball left OER on 30 June 2009.
bios.OER-2004-001:
Natalie Brooks was security and system integrity engineer from April 2004 to September 2006, the first in the role since Robert Ames left in March 2003. Brooks holds a B.S. in information systems with training in access control, audit procedures and configuration management, and came from access administration and change-control audits in a large enterprise computing environment.

Brooks believed an undocumented change is an operational risk even when nothing breaks, and disliked shared accounts and informal exceptions. Change records were checked against what was actually on the systems, and the person who approved a change was recorded separately from the person who carried it out. Brooks's notes often ended with the line "authorization confirmed; implementation still requires verification".

Brooks spent the first months on access reviews and audit trails left untended during the vacancy, and then on verifying the configuration changes of the cluster and video wall years. Brooks left OER on 30 September 2006, and David Coleman took over the role that October.
bios.OER-2004-002:
Catherine Doyle served as systems architect and technical lead from May 2004 to October 2010, the first architect since Rebecca Shaw left at the end of 2002. Doyle holds an MS in computer science and an undergraduate degree in computer engineering, and came from a distributed research computing program, designing service boundaries and coordinating technical decisions across separately managed systems.

Doyle was confident without being territorial, respected the systems inherited from the NEXUS years, and expected teams to explain undocumented behavior. Architecture diagrams were kept alongside implementation notes, each dependency was given an owner, and exceptions were written down before they could become permanent design.

Doyle approved 29 register revisions: the hot and cold aisles, FLR-001 E (October 2004), the second generator, PWR-005 A (May 2005), Row E for the blade chassis (August 2006), the 10 Gb core, NET-001 F (March 2007), 10 Gb wavelengths to Site B and four nodes, NET-002 G (November 2007), the staged SAN firmware of 2009 and MPLS between all sites, NET-002 H (June 2010). Doyle left in October 2010 for a senior architecture post in a larger distributed-systems program, and Michael Grant succeeded Doyle.
bios.OER-2004-003:
Phyllis Acosta served as Blue Crew Day Lead from May 2004 to the end of May 2007, following Harold Pruitt. Acosta grew up in Portland, Maine, had military technical training and an A.A.S. in electronics, and served four years as an Air Force communications specialist.

Imani Rhodes trained Acosta on the floor. Acosta loved a clean log, was steady under pressure and good at odd faults. Acosta had the floor on 13 August 2004 when Hurricane Charley crossed Florida and took Node 3 (Southeast) down for the evening, and led the Blue day shift when correlation moved to the Row D cluster in May 2004. Acosta trained Darren Caldwell and Russell Saldana.

Keith Espinoza was a close friend. Off shift: camping and hiking. Acosta left OER on 31 May 2007.
bios.OER-2004-004:
Keith Espinoza joined the Blue Crew as floater in June 2004 and sat Blue day Monitoring from September 2006 to the end of July 2008. Espinoza grew up in Kansas City, Missouri, earned an A.S. in Computer Networking, and worked as a help-desk technician at a manufacturer.

Imani Rhodes trained Espinoza, and Espinoza later took over Rhodes's Monitoring desk. Espinoza was steady under pressure and remembered past incidents in detail, which made the floater years useful: Espinoza could tell a new crew member what had happened the last time a tile did the same thing.

Espinoza was sociable and ran the break room. Phyllis Acosta was a close friend. Off shift: fishing and model building. Espinoza left OER on 31 July 2008.
bios.OER-2004-005:
James Holloway looked after OER's servers and infrastructure from September 2004 to November 2008, after the role had been vacant since Mike Dwyer left. Holloway holds a BS in information systems with Unix administration training, and came from a regional research computing center, maintaining Unix servers and storage across several facilities.

Holloway was dependable and understated, and preferred repairing a known system to replacing it without a tested migration path. Hardware and service notes were kept by host, recurring failures were recorded, and services were checked after maintenance rather than trusting a clean reboot.

Holloway drew 13 register revisions: the hot and cold aisle machine room, FLR-001 E, with its two added cooling units (October 2004); the second generator and its own plant drawing, PWR-005 A (May 2005); the retirement of the first host pair, RCK-01 D (April 2006); Row E and the first 64-bit multicore servers, RCK-05 A (August 2006); the tiered 300 TB SAN (February 2007); and the virtualization hosts for support services, RCK-05 B (May 2007). Holloway left in November 2008 for a broader systems engineering position, and Michelle Carter took over.
bios.OER-2004-006:
Ruth Gallagher owned external-feed operations from October 2004 to May 2009, after an extended vacancy following Marisol Vega's departure. Gallagher holds a BS in electrical engineering with training in telecommunications systems and network protocols, and came from a regional research network, maintaining leased lines, modem access and external data links for scattered sites.

Gallagher was calm under pressure and disliked replacing a working connection without understanding why it had failed. Paper notes sat beside the console with every provider contact name and escalation number, and after any repair the whole path was tested end to end.

Gallagher kept the older connections running while the feeds moved slowly toward internet delivery; in August 2007 severe weather warnings began arriving by internet alert feed, with the satellite receiver kept in service as backup. Gallagher left OER in May 2009 for a telecommunications engineering position with broader responsibilities, and Evan Brooks took over the feeds in 2010.
bios.OER-2004-007:
Marcus Bell was network and regional node engineer from November 2004 to July 2011, restoring a dedicated owner to the role after a long vacancy. Bell holds a BS in information technology with Cisco networking coursework, and came from a regional research and telecommunications network, maintaining routed links and remote-site connectivity.

Bell was calm and methodical and never assumed a remote node was dead just because it had stopped answering: alternate paths were checked first. Routing changes were recorded, and site-by-site connectivity notes were kept for each of the eight nodes and Site B. Failover testing became routine under Bell.

Bell drew five register revisions: the 10 Gb Ethernet core, NET-001 F (March 2007), 10 Gb wavelengths to Site B and Nodes 1, 2, 5 and 7, NET-002 G (November 2007), the replication checks before switching back from Site B, SITE-B-002 D (March 2008), MPLS between all sites, NET-002 H (June 2010), and the Site B consoles and video wall, SITE-B-001 D (November 2010). Bell left in July 2011 for a network architecture role, and Elena Vasquez took over in 2012.
bios.OER-2005-001:
Martin Shaw owned monitoring automation from July 2005 to February 2012, the first dedicated owner since Peter Sloane left in 2003. Shaw holds a BS in computer science with systems administration training, and came from systems automation in a distributed research computing environment, maintaining collection jobs, service checks and alert scripts across several sites.

Shaw was independent and cautious and disliked automation that hid failures or retried forever. A personal library of diagnostic scripts grew over the years, unusual exit codes were annotated, and the question was always whether a job had finished correctly, not just whether it had run.

Shaw maintained the old collection and alerting routines from the Sloane years while improving how failures were detected, through the cluster years and the arrival of the video wall in 2010. Shaw left in February 2012 for a senior systems automation position, and Anika Rao took over that December.
bios.OER-2005-002:
Sandra Lacey held the Red Crew day COMM seat from July 2005 to the end of August 2006. Lacey grew up in San Antonio, Texas, earned a B.S. in Business Administration at the University of Texas at San Antonio, and worked as a call-center trainer.

Joanne Tillman trained Lacey. Lacey was reserved, loyal and good at cross-checking records, and a natural teacher. Lacey joined the floor weeks before Katrina and Rita took Node 4 (Gulf / Texas) down, and was on duty for the leap second of 31 December 2005. Red Day COMM is the seat that speaks for the crew to the outside world, and Lacey took that seriously: calls were returned in order, every number was written down, and nothing went into the log that had not been confirmed. Lacey also helped train the next COMM operators on the phone procedures Tillman had built.

Off shift Lacey fished and quilted. Lacey left OER on 31 August 2006.
bios.OER-2005-003:
Charlene Tierney was the Red Crew floater from August 2005 to the end of November 2006. Tierney grew up in Cheyenne, Wyoming, earned an A.S. in Computer Networking, and worked as a data-center operator.

Joanne Tillman trained Tierney, who was earnest and careful, good at spotting small timing drifts and patient with new staff. Tierney covered the Red seats through the busy autumn of 2005 and the switch to proximity badges in October 2006. A floater on the Red crew learns all four seats and the crew's habits in each, and Tierney's quiet attention to detail made the handoffs smoother wherever Tierney sat. Tierney also helped the newer staff learn the board in the months after the second facility generator went into service, when the monthly generator tests briefly changed what a normal morning looked like.

Away from the floor Tierney painted and baked. Tierney left OER on 30 November 2006.
bios.OER-2005-004:
Darren Caldwell held the Blue Crew day Correlation seat from August 2005 to the end of January 2008. Caldwell grew up in Scranton, Pennsylvania, earned a B.S. in Electrical Engineering Technology at the University of Scranton, and worked as a production-control scheduler at a plant.

Phyllis Acosta trained Caldwell. Caldwell was laid-back, hard to rattle and good at odd faults, with a calm phone manner. Caldwell worked correlation through the switch to proximity badges in October 2006, the change to daylight saving time three weeks early in March 2007 and the arrival of severe weather warnings by internet alert feed that August.

Off shift Caldwell built models and was an amateur radio operator. Caldwell left OER on 31 January 2008.
bios.OER-2006-001:
Claire Donnelly was data quality and correlation engineer from January 2006 to October 2009, taking over the correlation work when Nora Whitcomb moved to data integration. Donnelly holds a BS in information systems with coursework in statistics and database design, and came from data validation at a large financial data-processing operation, investigating inconsistent transaction records.

Donnelly was patient with difficult data and skeptical of fixes that only hid the symptom, and was willing to challenge a source owner when the evidence supported it. A running exception list was kept, raw records were compared before any summary was accepted, and recurring edge cases were annotated.

Donnelly learned the cross-node correlation rules in the first years after correlation moved to the cluster, working closely with Whitcomb. Donnelly left in October 2009 for a senior data-quality position, and Alan Pierce took over in April 2010.
bios.OER-2006-002:
Elaine Brooks was reliability and performance engineer from September 2006 to June 2013, succeeding Tom Mercer. Brooks holds a B.S. in applied mathematics with computer systems coursework and training in capacity planning and statistical process analysis, and came from capacity planning and performance reporting for a large transaction-processing environment.

By 2006 OER's measurement history was long enough to show slow changes, and that was what Brooks was hired to read. Brooks was quietly persistent and skeptical of conclusions drawn from short windows, compared current figures with older baselines, annotated seasonal and workload effects, and kept notes on changes too small to trigger an alert.

Brooks checked 17 register revisions: the 10 Gb core (2007), compression on the node links, SWA-002 D (February 2008), overhead cable trays, FLR-001 G (March 2010), MPLS (June 2010), GPU correlation, SWA-001 G (June 2010), the thin-bezel video wall, FLR-002 E (November 2010), IPv6 and the removal of the dial-back modems, NET-005 B (August 2011), the UPS replacement (2012) and the leaf-spine fabric, NET-006 A (May 2013). Marcus Reed succeeded Brooks.
bios.OER-2006-003:
Russell Saldana joined the Blue Crew as floater in September 2006 and held the Blue day Correlation seat from April 2008 to the end of January 2020. Saldana grew up in Omaha, Nebraska, earned a B.S. in Environmental Science at the University of Nebraska Omaha, and led IT support for a school district.

Phyllis Acosta trained Saldana, who read everything twice and stayed steady under pressure. Saldana was on correlation on 21 October 2016, when an internet name-service outage cut five external feeds while regional node data kept flowing, and on 21 August 2017, when the eclipse showed up on the power grid tile region by region. Saldana trained Nathan Navarro, Bernadette Dempsey, Antoinette Oakley and Lorna Barlow.

Saldana kept standing lunches with Craig Lowry and Wayne Gutierrez. Off shift: photography and baking. Saldana left OER on 31 January 2020.
bios.OER-2006-004:
Tamara Ortiz held the Red Crew day COMM seat from September 2006 to the end of March 2007. Ortiz grew up in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, studied English at Duquesne University, and worked a hospital switchboard and telemetry desk.

Joanne Tillman trained Ortiz. Ortiz was quiet and watchful, wrote clear handoff notes and read ambiguous reports carefully. Ortiz started just as the floor moved to proximity badges and took the calls through the winter of 2006-07, including the early change to daylight saving time. COMM on the Red day crew means hearing about a regional problem first and saying only what has been confirmed, and Ortiz was good at both. The handoff notes from those months are short, exact and easy to pick up.

Off shift Ortiz painted and rode a bicycle. Ortiz left OER on 31 March 2007.
bios.OER-2006-005:
David Coleman was security and system integrity engineer from October 2006 to May 2008, following Natalie Brooks. Coleman holds a B.S. in information technology with training in Unix administration, access control and incident handling, and came from host security in a mixed-generation enterprise environment, including the cleanup of inherited administrative access.

Coleman was pragmatic: least privilege was the goal, but a poorly understood legacy dependency could make an immediate removal dangerous. Effective permissions were checked on the systems themselves rather than in the policy documents, a list was kept of exceptions still needing a reason, and Coleman noted any account whose purpose could no longer be established.

Coleman drew SEC-001 E, the OER-3 proximity cards that replaced the magnetic stripe badges on 2 October 2006, the day Coleman started. Coleman left OER on 31 May 2008.
bios.OER-2006-006:
Laura Bennett ran configuration and release from October 2006 to May 2010, following Graham Whitaker.
